<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS5" title="In 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.5 </span>Extension to long workflows on OSWorld-V2</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS6" title="In 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.6 </span>Pre-action verification under environment variation</span></a></li>

</ol></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hyewon Suh
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Thanh Minh Nguyen
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chih-Lun Lee
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Darrow Hartman
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Lizhao Liu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xin Eric Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ang Li
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jiachen Yang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_correspondent"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Corresponding author: </span>{hyewon, jiachen}@simular.ai
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Many computer tasks recur: the same workflow runs many times, with new inputs and from different starting states. Current computer-use agents re-plan every step of every run, which makes them costly and unreliable on such tasks. We introduce <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">neuro-symbolic computer use</em>, in which a recurring workflow is executed by a learned policy rather than re-derived by an agent on each run. The policy fixes the decisions that are stable across runs (ordering, variables, loops, and branches) in executable code, and delegates observation-dependent decisions, such as grounding and state checks, to neural models. We learn these policies with <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">neuro-symbolic policy iteration</em>: starting from one agent trajectory, it executes the policy, diagnoses failures with task-completion and step-level judges, and revises the code with a coding model informed by an agent’s continuation from the point of failure, without access to the benchmark evaluator. Iterating on generated parameter and initial-state variants makes the policy reusable, and a pre-action verifier guards each state-mutating step at deployment. On OSWorld-Verified and ScienceBoard, the learned policies achieve the highest Pass^3 of all methods in all four settings, 3.6–15.8 points above the base agent, while cutting per-run cost by 15–217<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and latency by 3.4–5.1<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>. On OSWorld-Verified, policies built only on variants transfer to the held-out original tasks, exceeding AutoRPA by 8.6–17.5 points in Pass^3.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="p2.1" class="ltx_quote ltx_epigraph " style="width:0pt; margin-left:auto;;">
<div id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_block ltx_epigraph_text" style="text-align:left; ;">
<p id="p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2.1.2" class="ltx_block ltx_epigraph_source" style="border-top:solid 0.4pt; text-align:right; ;">
<p id="p2.1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">— Alfred North Whitehead</span></p>
</div>
</blockquote>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A person who files expense reports a thousand times does not rediscover the same procedure on the thousandth attempt. However, contemporary computer-use agents still do: they plan step-by-step on every run, as if it were the first <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agashe et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agashe et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>. For economically-valuable recurring workflows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patwardhan et al., 2026</a>)</cite> where the same algorithmic procedure only needs limited decision-making, agents that plan from scratch on every step of every run face two critical problems: unreliability over repeated runs of the same task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, and high cost and latency of frontier-model calls on long workflows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. How can an agent turn execution experience into a reusable procedure that stays reliable and efficient as inputs and states vary?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing ways to automate such workflows sit at two extremes. At the neural extreme, computer-use agents decide every action from the current observation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agashe et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. They are flexible, but re-decide steps that never change, so every run is costly and lacks reliability. At the symbolic extreme, robotic process automation (RPA) runs a recorded or hand-written script <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Van der Aalst et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, which is cheap to repeat but breaks when a states changes and does not generalize beyond anticipated cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To solve this dilemma, we introduce the paradigm of <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use</span>, in which a recurring workflow is executed by a learned neuro-symbolic policy instead of being re-derived by an agent on every run. Our core insight is that recurring workflows contain a mixture of deterministic transitions and state-dependent decisions, and that neuro-symbolic programs are reliable and efficient <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">representations</em> of such workflows. In expense reporting for example, form fields almost never change, but the location of a “submit” button may vary and a check for login may be needed. We therefore represent the procedure as a neuro-symbolic policy: code fixes the stable decisions (algorithm, variables, and control flow), while neural primitives make state-dependent decisions at run time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To learn such policies, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration (NSPI)</span>, which synthesizes an initial policy from a base neural agent’s demonstration trajectories and refines it by iterating between policy evaluation and policy improvement without ground truth rewards (<a href="#S2.F1" title="In 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). A task-completion judge checks the end state of each iteration’s policy rollout, and a step-level judge locates the first step that went wrong. Upon a failure verdict, an agent continues the task from the failed state, and a coding model revises the policy using this continuation and the judges’ diagnosis. This execute–diagnose–explore–revise loop repeats until every rollout in an iteration passes or the budget runs out. At convergence, the policy itself represents a summary of the learned experience, and only here does it receive feedback from the benchmark evaluator. To test generalizability we also refine it on task variants, before its deployment along with a pre-action verifier guarding each state-mutating action against environment drift.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate NSPI on three properties that recurring workflows require: reliability across repeated runs, reuse on similar task instances, and efficiency. On OSWorld-Verified (henceforth OSWorld) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and ScienceBoard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite> with GPT-5.6 Terra and Claude Opus 5 as base agent models, the learned policies achieve the highest Pass^3 (the share of tasks solved in all three runs) of all methods in all four settings, 4.5–13.9 points above the base agent. We also learn policies only on synthetic OSWorld variants that change a task’s parameters or its starting state, and evaluate them on the held-out original tasks, where they exceed AutoRPA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on the same task families by 8.6-17.5 points in Pass^3. Because a learned policy does not re-derive the workflow, it runs 15–217<math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> cheaper and 3.4–5.1<math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the base agent, and the one-time cost of learning it is recovered after 3–27 runs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use</h2>

<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/overview_fin_update_to_policy.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/164;" width="476" height="164"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
<span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Recurring</span> computer workflows require reliable repeated execution with generalizability at low cost. In <span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration</span>: a baseline agent’s exploration seeds an initial neuro-symbolic policy, which preserves the workflow’s stable structure in code while retaining neural primitives for observation-dependent decisions. Our framework iteratively executes, evaluates, diagnoses, and improves the policy with additional agent continuation. The resulting policy is reused across workflows and guarded with pre-action verifiers during run-time deployment.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Problem statement: recurring workflows and reusable policies</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider recurring parametric computer tasks on open-world desktop environments, a common setting in personal logistics and business processes. A task <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is a natural-language instruction to be completed in a digital environment (a desktop application or a website) with transition function <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> and initial state distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. Executing a policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> from an initial state <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}\sim\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}\sim\rho</annotation></semantics></math> produces a trajectory <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},\dotsc,o_{|\tau|})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},\dotsc,o_{|\tau|})</annotation></semantics></math> of observations and actions. A held-out success indicator <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(\tau;g)\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(\tau;g)\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., the evaluation script of a benchmark or a user’s unknown preferences) determines whether <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> completed <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>. We require a policy for each <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> to succeed across a parameterized family <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> of task instances similar to <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., “book a flight on {date}”) and across initial states <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}\sim\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}\sim\rho</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Objective and reliability metric.</span> We seek a policy that maximizes reliability over the task family:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mathcal{G}}\big[\text{{Pass\textasciicircum k}}(\pi;g)\big]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>π</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.447em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mtext>Pass^k</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mathcal{G}}\big[\text{{Pass\textasciicircum k}}(\pi;g)\big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where Pass^k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is the probability that all <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> independent executions of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> succeed:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle p_{\pi}(g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle p_{\pi}(g)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho,\,\tau\sim(\pi,T)}\big[R(\tau;g)\big]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo lspace="0em">=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho,\,\tau\sim(\pi,T)}\big[R(\tau;g)\big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Given <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> executions with <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> successes, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is the unbiased estimator of Pass^k for any <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\leq n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\leq n</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Amortized cost metric.</span> Let <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> be the one-time cost (in dollars or wall-clock time) of constructing <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> its cost per execution; the amortized cost per execution over <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> executions is</p>
<table id="S2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bar{c}_{\pi}(n)\vcentcolon=\frac{C_{\pi}}{n}+c_{\pi}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bar{c}_{\pi}(n)\vcentcolon=\frac{C_{\pi}}{n}+c_{\pi}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">A pure neural agent <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\mu}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\mu}=0</annotation></semantics></math> (ignoring the costs of model training) but a high <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> if it calls an expensive LLM to plan every step. In general, a policy <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\pi}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\pi}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> and a lower <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> would have lower amortized cost once <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds the break-even point <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{\ast}=C_{\pi}/(c_{\mu}-c_{\pi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{\ast}=C_{\pi}/(c_{\mu}-c_{\pi})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Neuro-symbolic policies</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A neuro-symbolic policy is a program <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> in a scripting language whose statements are control flow (loops, conditionals, variable assignment, and recursion) and calls to primitives from a set <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\text{neu}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mtext>sym</mtext></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mtext>neu</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\text{neu}}</annotation></semantics></math> (detailed in <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Primitive action space ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>). We write <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi</annotation></semantics></math> for the class of policies defined by such programs. Symbolic primitives in <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mtext>sym</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}</annotation></semantics></math>, such as keyboard shortcuts, shell commands, and file operations, execute without a model call. Neural primitives in <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\text{neu}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mtext>neu</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\text{neu}}</annotation></semantics></math> call a model on the current observation <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and our work includes: 1) GUI grounding actions (e.g., <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;">click(description)</span>) map natural-language element descriptions to screen coordinates using a visual grounding model; 2) a condition check <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(\phi,o_{t})\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(\phi,o_{t})\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, e.g., <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{stateSatisfies(condition)}\rightarrow\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;" mathcolor="#005078">stateSatisfies(condition)</mtext><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;" mathcolor="#005078" stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;" mathcolor="#005078">0</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;" mathcolor="#005078">,</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#005078;" mathcolor="#005078">1</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{stateSatisfies(condition)}\rightarrow\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, returns whether <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies a natural-language condition <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, and the control flow of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> can branch on its output. All neural primitives include the accessibility tree and the screenshot in <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> as input by default, so the policy only needs to represent natural language inputs. <a href="#S2.F2" title="In 2.2 Neuro-symbolic policies ‣ 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows an example policy before and after refinement. At deployment, the program runtime applies each state-mutating primitive with the pre-action verifier of <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Pre-action verification ‣ 3.2 Policy generalization ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/code_policy_example_v2.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/148;" width="476" height="148"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
Example of NSPI converting agent trajectory into a reusable, abstracted neuro-symbolic policy and using judge feedback to identify and heal failures. The resulting policy combines state-dependent control flow, task parameters in code, and neural primitives for grounding
(<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>).
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">NSPI first learns a policy that solves a task reliably (<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Policy learning ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>) and then generalizes it beyond the instance it was learned on (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Policy generalization ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>); <a href="#S2.F1" title="In 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows both parts.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Policy learning</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Synthesis and iterative refinement</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy iteration.</span> We search <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi</annotation></semantics></math> for a policy that maximizes <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.1 Problem statement: recurring workflows and reusable policies ‣ 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> by policy iteration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howard, 1960</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton and Barto, 2018</a>)</cite>, which alternates between policy evaluation and policy improvement. A dual judge evaluates the policy (<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS2" title="3.1.2 Policy evaluation with a dual judge ‣ 3.1 Policy learning ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.2</span></a>), and a code healer improves it (<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS3" title="3.1.3 Policy improvement with a code healer ‣ 3.1 Policy learning ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.3</span></a>). Together, the two judges are the analog of the critic in policy iteration. Despite not being fit to ground-truth rewards like a classical critic, they rely on the knowledge of the underlying LLMs to produce an evaluation of the current policy in natural language.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initialization.</span> Given a task <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, a base agent <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> produces a trajectory <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>, which need not be successful. A converter <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{\text{conv}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{\text{conv}}</annotation></semantics></math> turns <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> into the initial policy <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(0)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(0)}</annotation></semantics></math>: it concatenates the agent’s actions into a single program, replaces pixel coordinates with natural-language descriptions of the target elements that the runtime grounds at execution time, and replaces values specific to <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> with task parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Iteration.</span> At iteration <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we execute <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> up to <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> times, each from a freshly reset initial state, and judge each rollout <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{(i)}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{(i)}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> with the dual judge of <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS2" title="3.1.2 Policy evaluation with a dual judge ‣ 3.1 Policy learning ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.2</span></a> (policy evaluation). If all <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> rollouts pass the judge, we return <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Otherwise, we stop at the first failed rollout and produce <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(i+1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(i+1)}</annotation></semantics></math> with the code healer of <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS3" title="3.1.3 Policy improvement with a code healer ‣ 3.1 Policy learning ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.3</span></a> (policy improvement). The loop runs for at most <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> iterations and returns the last policy if no iteration passes. Note again that <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> is not used; we apply it only the returned policy to measure Pass^k. Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Iteration ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a> gives further details of the loop.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Policy evaluation with a dual judge</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate each policy rollout with two judges to detect and localize failures and provide diagnosis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task-completion judge.</span> The task-completion judge <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a VLM agent that receives only the task <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> (and the answer submitted by the policy, for question-answering tasks) and probes the end state of the machine with read-only tools, such as shell commands and file reads. It returns a verdict <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\text{task}}\in\{\text{success},\text{failure},\text{abstain}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>success</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>failure</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>abstain</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\text{task}}\in\{\text{success},\text{failure},\text{abstain}\}</annotation></semantics></math> with the evidence <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> it collected, and it abstains when success depends on transient states during task execution; an applicability gate skips it for tasks whose success cannot be checked from persistent state.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step-level judge.</span> The step-level judge runs on every rollout, in parallel with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and has two stages. First, for each transition <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, an observer VLM describes the change between consecutive observations, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}=J_{\text{obs}}(o_{t},o_{t+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>obs</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}=J_{\text{obs}}(o_{t},o_{t+1})</annotation></semantics></math>, without access to the task, the code, or the stated intent of the step, so that each description is based only on observable evidence. Second, a localizer VLM reads the task, the policy, and all observer outputs, and returns a verdict, the first step at which the rollout diverged from the task, and a named failure mode, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(v_{\text{loc}},t^{\ast},m)=J_{\text{loc}}(g,\pi,\delta_{0:|\tau|-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v_{\text{loc}},t^{\ast},m)=J_{\text{loc}}(g,\pi,\delta_{0:|\tau|-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verdict and diagnostic.</span> A rollout passes only if <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\text{loc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\text{loc}}</annotation></semantics></math> is success and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is success or <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> was skipped by the applicability gate, so an abstention by <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> counts as a failure. An aggregator LLM composes the outputs of both judges, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v_{\text{task}},e_{\text{task}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v_{\text{task}},e_{\text{task}})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v_{\text{loc}},t^{\ast},m)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v_{\text{loc}},t^{\ast},m)</annotation></semantics></math>, into a diagnostic <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> for the healer. We measure how often the judges agree with the benchmark evaluation scripts in Section <a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 Judge Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>. <a href="#alg1" title="In A.4 Dual judge ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> states the procedure, and Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Dual judge ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a> gives the details of both judges.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>Policy improvement with a code healer</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When rollout <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{(i)}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{(i)}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> fails, the base agent <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> continues the task from the end state of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{(i)}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{(i)}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, given <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, the policy <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, its execution log, and the diagnostic <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, and produces a continuation <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{cont}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>cont</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{cont}}</annotation></semantics></math>. A summarizer LLM <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{\text{sum}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>sum</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{\text{sum}}</annotation></semantics></math> condenses it into a short description of the actions that made progress. The healer <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{\text{heal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>heal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{\text{heal}}</annotation></semantics></math>, a coding LLM, then rewrites the policy:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\pi^{(i+1)}=\Phi_{\text{heal}}\big(\pi^{(i)},\tau^{(i)}_{j},d,\Phi_{\text{sum}}(\tau_{\text{cont}});g\big)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>heal</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>sum</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>cont</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\pi^{(i+1)}=\Phi_{\text{heal}}\big(\pi^{(i)},\tau^{(i)}_{j},d,\Phi_{\text{sum}}(\tau_{\text{cont}});g\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{(i)}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{(i)}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> enters as its execution log, error message, and a subset of its screenshots. Upon execution errors, we skip the judges and agent continuation, giving the error directly to the healer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Policy generalization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">NSPI generalizes to anticipated task variations by running policy iteration on generated variants that perturb the task’s parameters and initial state, so that the healer must write code that reads the parameters of the instance and handles each initial state (<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Robust learning under workflow perturbations ‣ 3.2 Policy generalization ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>). <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Policy generalization across workflow instances ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> tests generalization to held-out tasks. Unanticipated environment nonstationarity are caught at deployment by a pre-action verifier, which can hand the task to a general agent or escalate it for human review in sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance (<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Pre-action verification ‣ 3.2 Policy generalization ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Robust learning under workflow perturbations</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a target task <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct variants of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> in two categories of workflow variation, run policy iteration on the variants, and hold out <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> itself for evaluation (<a href="#A2.F7" title="In B.2.1 Task variant generation ‣ B.2 Workflow Variation ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initial-state variants</span> keep the instruction of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and start the environment in a different realistic state, e.g., the target document is closed, a dialog blocks the window, or the output file already holds stale values. We run the base agent on natural language instructions to set up such initial states. <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parameter variants</span> keep the initial state of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and change the argument values in its instruction, e.g., a date, a count, a file name, or a setting value. An LLM proposes multiple variants per category, and a validator rejects any that changes the goal of the task or the content of taks setup files. Task variants are presented to NSPI sequentially, thereby exposing hard-coded values and unhandled states, forcing the policy to avoid overfitting any single variant. <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> describes the variants we construct for each benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Pre-action verification</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We check the precondition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fikes and Nilsson, 1971</a>)</cite> of every state-mutating primitive using a fast and calibrated VLM classifier before deploying the final policy (<a href="#A1.F6" title="In A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inputs and outputs.</span> The verifier <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> receives the task, the primitive action (function call with inputs), a natural-language explanation of the step from the policy’s in-line comments at (or before) the action, current observation, and the primitives already executed in this run (<a href="#A1.E5" title="In A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>), and it either passes or blocks the primitive. On a block, the particular application setting may choose among handing the task to a stateful agent to continue, running NSPI, or escalating to a human.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decision rule.</span> We prompt a VLM to answer with one token, yes if the action should run now and no otherwise, following a fixed rubric (Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>). The verifier blocks when <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the renormalized probability mass of the no answers among the 20 most likely tokens, reaches a threshold <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> set on a calibration set (<a href="#A1.E6" title="In A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>). Using <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math> instead of the greedy answer turns the trade-off between wrong blocks and wrong passes into a single parameter <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments and Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on OSWorld-Verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and ScienceBoard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We use 361 OSWorld tasks, excluding Google Drive tasks that require unavailable credentials, and 169 ScienceBoard tasks spanning six scientific desktop applications. Further evaluation settings are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Main experiment configuration ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>. We also explore longer workflows on OSWorld-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>)</cite> as a separate extension (<a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Extension to long workflows on OSWorld-V2 ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compared methods</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using GPT-5.6 Terra <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>)</cite> and Claude Opus 5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>)</cite> as backbone models, we compare our method with three baselines. The <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base agent</span> plans each action from the current observation and solves each task anew on every run, without retaining experience across runs. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Batch2Code</span> is a conversion-only variant of NSPI that uses the same code-policy without iterative refinement. It constructs the policy from multiple base-agent trajectories, giving it more initial trajectory evidence than our single-trajectory initialization. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ASI</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> acquires reusable programmatic skills while retaining an agent to select and execute them. For reuse across parameter and initial-state variations, we compare with <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoRPA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, adapted to learn reusable computer-use workflows from natural-language requests and execution experience, without benchmark-supplied task templates, parameter schemas, or oracle feedback. Further details on experiment setups and configurations are included in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Main experiment configuration ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Workflow variation</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate whether a learned policy transfers to a held-out instance of the same workflow. We constructed the workflow variations of the subset of OSWorld tasks. Parameter variants change request arguments, while initial-state variants preserve the request but alter the starting environment. We study 40 parameter and 35 initial-state families with up to three admitted variants. NSPI and AutoRPA both use GPT-5.6 Terra and a shared domain setup, without access to the benchmark evaluator. They process the same variants sequentially, refining a single policy as new instances expose task-specific assumptions. We then freeze the policy and evaluate Pass^3 on the held-out original task without further adaptation. We include implementation details in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Workflow Variation ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report Pass^k for <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,2,3\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{1,2,3\}</annotation></semantics></math>, estimated from three evaluation trials per task as defined in <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Problem statement: recurring workflows and reusable policies ‣ 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>; Pass^3 measures success in all three trials. We average over the full task or family set, retaining construction failures in the denominator. We report per-execution cost and wall-clock latency separately from one-time construction cost and time, and analyze their amortization over repeated use (<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Efficient repeated execution and cost amortization ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Reliability across repeated executions</h3>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<span id="S4.T1.2.20.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E2F0D9;">
<span id="S4.T1.2.20.6.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T1.2.20.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline" style="font-size:90%;">103</span></span>
