</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>
Reliability across repeated executions on ScienceBoard and OSWorld. Per-run cost (USD) and wall-clock latency for NSPI and as relative multiples (<math id="S4.T1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>) of NSPI for other methods. NSPI achieves the highest Pass^3 in all four settings while operating at substantially lower per-run cost. Batch2Code, a conversion-only variant of our framework is also efficient, but with substantially lower Pass^k.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.2 Reliability across repeated executions ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows a clear reliability gap under repeated execution. Averaged across the four benchmark–model settings, NSPI drops only 3.4 points from Pass^1 to Pass^3, compared with 12.4 points for the base agent, and achieves the highest Pass^3 in every setting, by 8.1 points on average over the next-best method. Its Pass^1 remains comparable to the base agent, so the flatter curve is not obtained by starting from a weaker policy. NSPI can also bootstrap from unsuccessful demonstrations. Across 356 tasks for which the base agent failed all three seed attempts, the final policy succeeds in Pass^3 on 62 tasks, including 32 of 89 on ScienceBoard with Opus (Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Reliability across repeated executions ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). This recovery requires more refinement, with failed seeds incurring 18–31% higher healing cost and 17–38% longer healing time than successful seeds. We provide the full breakdown in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Constructing Policies from Unsuccessful Trajectories ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The comparison with Batch2Code helps distinguish reliable execution from simply making execution more deterministic. Batch2Code uses the same executable policy representation without iterative refinement, and its Pass^k curve is similarly flat, but its Pass^3 remains 3.3–33.1 points below NSPI. Code therefore helps preserve a procedure across runs, while refinement makes it consistently correct. ASI, which instead retains an agent to select and execute learned programmatic skills, shows a decline with repeated execution closer to the base agent. Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Reliability across repeated executions ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates the same trade-off on ScienceBoard with GPT-5.6 Terra. NSPI maintains its success rate as <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> increases while moving execution to a much lower-cost regime. Across all four settings, the resulting policies reduce per-run cost by 15-217x and run 3.4–5.1× faster than the corresponding base agents.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F3.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F3.2.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/main_passk_sb_terra.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:210/147;" width="210" height="147"></object></span><span id="S4.F3.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_align_left ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:80%;width:0.0pt;position:relative; bottom:105.9pt;">(a)</span> <span id="S4.F3.2.3" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/main_cost_sb_terra.svg" id="S4.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:210/144;" width="210" height="144"></object></span><span id="S4.F3.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_align_left ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:80%;width:0.0pt;position:relative; bottom:103.6pt;">(b)</span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
Repeated-execution reliability and execution cost on ScienceBoard with GPT-5.6-Terra.
(a) NSPI maintains high Pass^k as k increases, while agent-based baselines degrade more sharply and the Batch2Code conversion-only baseline remains consistent but less accurate. (b) NSPI achieves highest Pass^3 with efficient per-run execution cost over baselines. </figcaption>
</figure>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Policy generalization across workflow instances</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate reuse across workflow instances on OSWorld with GPT-5.6 Terra, refining one policy on generated variants and evaluating the frozen policy on the held-out original task. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Policy generalization across workflow instances ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, NSPI reaches 55.0% Pass^3 on parameter variations and 60.0% on initial-state variations, compared with 37.5% and 51.4% for AutoRPA. Both methods degrade a little from Pass^1 to Pass^3, suggesting that the dominant challenge is whether a learned policy transfers to a workflow instance at all, rather than stochastic failure once it does. NSPI’s advantage comes primarily from transferring successfully to more workflow instances.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Policy generalization across workflow instances ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> examines which policy structures are associated with successful transfer. For parameterized workflows, policies that read changing values from the request transfer much more often than policies that retain training values, supporting the need to separate stable workflow structure from instance-specific inputs. For initial-state variation, policies that modify application files or use command-line interfaces transfer more often than GUI-only policies for both methods, consistent with being less dependent on the precise starting GUI state. AutoRPA relies on these script-based paths more heavily, yet NSPI performs better within both execution styles, so its advantage is not simply due to bypassing the GUI. Overall, successful reuse appears to depend on preserving the procedure while rebinding the parts that vary with the current request or environment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.SS3.fig1" class="ltx_figure">

Effectiveness of policy built across parameter and initial state variations to held-out instances of OSWorld workflows.
</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:155.3pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>
Policy structures associated with successful reuse across workflow instances. Labels show the number of successful policies out of total applicable policies.
</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Efficient repeated execution and cost amortization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the economics of neuro-symbolic policies using Eq. (<a href="#S2.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 2.1 Problem statement: recurring workflows and reusable policies ‣ 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Efficient repeated execution and cost amortization ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the resulting costs. Across different configurations, neuro-symbolic policy’s per-execution cost ratio <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\mu}/c_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\mu}/c_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> ranges from roughly 15<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> to roughly 217<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and policies recover their construction cost between 3.1 and 26.8 executions. The break-even points in wall-clock time range between 8.6 and 16.9 executions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results also indicate that the benefit of NSPI scales with task complexity. Moving from ScienceBoard to OSWorld increases the agent’s per-run dollar cost by four to six times, while construction cost increases by only 14% to 52%. The break-even point drops nearly 75% in dollar value. The choice of a base model has a similar effect in dollar value. Claude Opus 5 incurs two to three times the construction cost of GPT-5.6 Terra, but its per-run agent cost is four to six times higher, so in dollars it breaks even roughly 2 to 2.4 times sooner. In wall-clock time, the two models are much closer. We note that these comparisons span only two benchmarks and two base models, so task complexity is partially confounded with other differences between benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>
Cost and wall-clock latency amortization of learning a reusable NSPI in the terms of <a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.1 Problem statement: recurring workflows and reusable policies ‣ 2 Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> is the one-time policy-construction cost, <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> the per-run cost of the base agent, <math id="S4.T3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> the per-run cost of executing the learned policy, and <math id="S4.T3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the break-even count. Values are means over tasks.
</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Extension to long workflows on OSWorld-V2</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We stress-tested NSPI on OSWorld-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, where tasks take skilled humans more than an hour on average and cost frontier-model agents up to $76 and 50 minutes per task. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span> shows that the learned policies are more consistent than the base agent but less successful. On strict success, NSPI keeps 96% of its Pass^1 at <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k{=}3</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas the base agent keeps only 80%. However, NSPI trails the base agent at <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> by 5.6 points in strict success and by 18.5 points in partial credit. The gap in performance arises from a loss of information in converting a long agent trajectory to initial policy: agent trajectories averaged 158 steps and scripts averaged 970 lines, leading to mistakes when the script recomputes every value the agent read from the screen. Implementation details are available in <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 OSWorld-V2 extension ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Pre-action verification under environment variation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the pre-action verifier (<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Pre-action verification ‣ 3.2 Policy generalization ‣ 3 Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>) with the injected intent comments and rubric additions of Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Precondition checks ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> at <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.78</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0.78</annotation></semantics></math>. The <em id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">wrong-block rate</em> (WBR) is the fraction of rollouts of correct policies in which the verifier incorrectly blocks at least one primitive. The <em id="S4.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">wrong-pass rate</em> (WPR) is the fraction of primitives that should be blocked but that the verifier passes. We simulate an unexpected environment change by running the correct policies of original OSWorld tasks but starting from the perturbed initial states of the generalization experiment (<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Policy generalization across workflow instances ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), which yields 24 primitives that should be blocked. <a href="#A2.F8" title="In B.4 Precondition checks ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B wrongly blocks at most 8.4% of correct rollouts in every setting, while Qwen3.8-27B wrongly blocks 9.4–25.0%. The trade-off reverses on the perturbed initial states: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has WPR 70.8% (17 of 24 primitives passed), while Qwen3.8-27B has WPR 25.0% (6 of 24). Median verifier latency is <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5\text{s}\pm 0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\text{s}\pm 0.5</annotation></semantics></math> (p95 <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.3\text{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.3\text{s}</annotation></semantics></math>) for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.6\text{s}\pm 1.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1.6</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.6\text{s}\pm 1.2</annotation></semantics></math> (p95 <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.7\text{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.7</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.7\text{s}</annotation></semantics></math>) for Qwen3.8-27B.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Judge Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T5" title="In 4.7 Judge Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> compares our judges with the benchmark evaluator on each task’s final policy, where a policy is reliable only if it succeeds in all three runs. The judges reject 69.3–94.4% of unreliable policies but accept only 11.4–40.1% of reliable ones. They are therefore conservative, which increases construction cost without hurting reliability. A better-calibrated judge could lower this cost and potentially improve performance, which we leave to future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also annotate 19 OSWorld policies rejected by <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> and compare both judges with human labels (<a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Judge analysis details ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>). <a href="#S4.T6" title="In 4.7 Judge Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> agrees closely with human annotators, and so does <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{loc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{loc}}</annotation></semantics></math> on divergence localization when the evidence is visible on screen. We discuss four limitations of the judges in the same appendix.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior methods on learning skills from experience enable an agent to accumulate a library of reusable APIs, represented either in natural language <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> or as short programs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ning et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. We take this approach to the limit by aiming for a single robust code policy that solves each equivalence set of parametric tasks in full. While the neural agent is the primary driver that invokes skills in prior work, our neuro-symbolic policy is primary while the agent is an expensive fallback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Programs with perceptual inputs have long served as policies, from programmatic reinforcement learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Verma et al., 2018</a>)</cite> to LLM-generated robot code <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Santos et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. The LLM-generated policies were produced from human natural language instructions and few-shot examples, instead of from a strong agent exploration as in our work. They were also static, whereas our neuro-symbolic iterative refinement method allows the policy to improve over time based on execution feedback and continual agent exploration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The most similar prior work is AutoRPA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which converts ReAct-style agent exploration into replayable RPA scripts with iterative refinement, demonstrating substantial cost reduction while maintaining baseline pass@1 success rate. Our work differs in that our method explicitly optimizes Pass^k success rate and realistic intra-task generalization to different task parameters and initial states, along with a precondition check for practical deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced neuro-symbolic computer use as a way to turn execution experience into reusable policies for recurring workflows, preserving stable procedure in code while leaving state-dependent decisions to neural primitives. Neuro-Symbolic Policy Iteration learns these policies from agent trajectories through execution, diagnosis, exploration, and revision, and further refines them across task-parameter and initial-state variations. Across OSWorld and ScienceBoard, the resulting policies improve reliability under repeated execution while substantially reducing per-run cost and latency, and they transfer more successfully than AutoRPA to held-out instances of the same workflow. Results on longer-horizon tasks and our judge and verifier analyses also expose remaining bottlenecks in trajectory-to-policy conversion and policy evaluation, suggesting that better acquisition and verification could further extend this approach to more complex recurring workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Method details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Primitive action space</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate policies in Simulang <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simular AI, 2026</a>)</cite>, a scripting language for desktop and web automation in the style of PyAutoGUI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sweigart, 2014</a>)</cite> and Playwright <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft, 2020</a>)</cite> that also provides the neural primitives above. <a href="#A1.T7" title="In A.1 Primitive action space ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> lists the primitives that the converter and the healer can use on ScienceBoard. The healer can combine them with Python control flow, e.g., a loop that retries a click or a branch on <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">state_satisfies</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>
Primitive action space of policies on ScienceBoard.
Each primitive is a method of an <span id="A1.T7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">agent</span> object that the policy calls, e.g., <span id="A1.T7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">agent.click("File menu")</span>.
Neural primitives call a model on the current observation <math id="A1.T7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>: the grounded actions use UI-Venus-1.5-30B-A3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2026</a>)</cite> with a consensus over three parallel calls, and the condition check uses Gemini 3 Flash.
A check mark under <em id="A1.T7.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Mut.</em> marks a primitive that changes the state of the computer; these count toward the per-task step budget and are gated by the pre-action verifier.
</figcaption>

<span id="A1.T7.8.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T7.8.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Primitive</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T7.8.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><span id="A1.T7.8.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Mut.</span></td>
<td id="A1.T7.8.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;">

<td id="A1.T7.8.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><span id="A1.T7.8.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>

<span id="A1.T7.8.19.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T7.8.19.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ends the plan and submits </span><span id="A1.T7.8.19.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">x</span><span id="A1.T7.8.19.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, which the evaluator matches exactly, for question-answering tasks.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T7.8.20" class="ltx_tr">

</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Initialization</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The base agent <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> runs on <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> in exploration mode, in which actions may be arbitrary code, and we record its trajectory <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>. The converter <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{\text{conv}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{\text{conv}}</annotation></semantics></math> first extracts the discrete actions of <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> into a single contiguous script (Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). It then replaces pixel coordinates, which were recorded on a different machine and are unreliable, with natural-language descriptions of the target elements that the runtime grounds at execution time, and it replaces values specific to <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> with task parameters. On ScienceBoard, this second step is one LLM call that receives the task, the extracted script, and a screenshot and accessibility tree of the initial state. On OSWorld, the base agent trajectory was based on Agent-S3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> which already encodes the trajectory in semantic-level rather than pixel-level, then calls an LLM for the final conversion. Conditioning <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{\text{conv}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{\text{conv}}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> lets it drop incidental actions in <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>, such as backtracking, exploratory clicks, and redundant verifications, so that they are not transcribed into the code policy that will be refined.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Iteration</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rollouts within an iteration run in a random order, and the iteration stops at the first rollout that fails the judge, so the agent continuation runs at most once per iteration. Every code rollout and every agent continuation is capped at the task’s step budget, i.e., the maximum number of state-mutating actions, which matches the budget of the baseline agent; the localizer and the healer are told the budget so that their suggestions fit within it. The agent continuation can use GUI actions and run Python or shell commands on the machine, and it receives the output of those commands in later turns. The continuation is not judged and does not change the verdict of the code rollout; it serves only as experience for the healer. A rollout that raises a code execution error (a syntax error, an undefined name, a failed import, etc.) produces no trajectory for the judges to grade, so we skip the judges and the continuation and give the traceback to the healer. The healer receives at most five screenshots of the failed rollout, sampled evenly over the trajectory, and it rewrites the whole code policy. The converter and the healer are instructed to prefer programmatic actions (shell commands, Python, and application command lines) over long sequences of GUI actions, which replaces neural primitives with symbolic ones and lowers the cost per execution <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, although our method does not optimize cost directly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Motivation for two judges.</span> Evaluating a computer-use rollout is harder than reading an exit code, for two reasons. First, an agent’s own report of what it did is often optimistic, e.g., it may report that it clicked a button while the screen shows that the click missed, or that it entered a value into a spreadsheet cell while it edited the wrong cell, so an evaluator that trusts the actor’s narrative inherits its errors. Second, benchmark evaluation scripts such as those of OSWorld check the end state of the environment (the contents of a saved spreadsheet, an exported image, the browser’s bookmarks, etc.), which an evaluator that only watches the trajectory cannot see. For example, a LibreOffice Calc plan that types the correct formula but closes the window before the file is saved, a GIMP plan whose edit is never exported to the target file, and a Chrome plan whose bookmark fails to persist all look correct frame by frame, yet all fail the evaluation script. The task completion judge addresses the second problem, and the step-level judge addresses the first while also localizing the error for the healer. We ablate the two judges in Section <a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 Judge Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task completion judge.</span> <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a VLM agent with read-only probes of the live machine: shell commands, file reads, directory listings, SQL queries over application databases, and screenshots. Mutating shell commands are rejected by a deny-list, and databases are opened read-only. <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> receives only the task description (and the submitted answer for question-answering tasks), and never another judge’s verdict or the benchmark’s verdict. It decomposes the goal into verifiable sub-conditions, probes the machine until it can settle each one (preferring filesystem and database probes over screenshots), and returns a verdict with supporting evidence within a budget of 30 tool calls and 300 seconds. It abstains (<span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cannot_verify</span>) when the state needed to check success is transient or depends on context that is not persisted, e.g., for “move the file back where it used to be”, the original path no longer exists. <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is not a ground-truth oracle, because its verdict is only as good as the probes it chooses to run; this is why an abstention falls back to the step-level judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Applicability gate.</span> One VLM call on the task instruction, cached per task, decides whether success can be checked from persistent machine state. If not, <math id="A1.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is skipped and the verdict comes from the step-level judge alone, which spends no probe budget on a question <math id="A1.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> could not answer.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observers.</span> For GUI primitives, the evidence for transition <math id="A1.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is the pair of screenshots before and after the step, together with the difference between accessibility trees when available. For primitives that leave no visual trace, e.g., API calls, background shell commands, or functions executed inside the code runtime, the evidence is the return value, exit code, and captured output, and no screen change is expected. Each observer returns an objective description of what the step produced and an anomaly grade. Observers do not see the task, the code, or the stated intent of the step, because an observer told that the agent intended to save a file can no longer distinguish “the agent believes it saved” from “the file was saved”, which is the distinction the evaluation script checks. The <math id="A1.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\tau|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\tau|</annotation></semantics></math> observer calls are independent and run in parallel.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Localizer.</span> The localizer is one VLM call that receives the task, the executed code, and the ordered observer outputs, but not the actor’s narrative. It enumerates the sub-goals of the task and checks each against the observer evidence. It also screens for composition failures, i.e., sequences of individually plausible steps that together are incoherent or destructive, such as an action that is immediately undone, a target value that is overwritten, or a save followed by closing the application before the write completed. It returns the verdict, the first divergent step <math id="A1.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a name for the failure mode, which the healer uses when rewriting the code policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diagnostic.</span> An LLM composes the outputs of both judges into the diagnostic <math id="A1.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="A1.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> lists each judge’s observations (the probe results of <math id="A1.SS4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the observer descriptions) separately from its interpretations (verdicts, failure hypotheses, and suggested focus), and it tells the healer that observations are facts about the machine while verdicts can be wrong.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Pre-action verifier</h3>

<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/verifier_v2.svg" id="A1.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/176;" width="476" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>
A learned binary-output pre-action verifier <math id="A1.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> runs before every state-mutating primitive during policy deployment. Reusing the plan’s most recent stashed screenshot and accessibility tree, <math id="A1.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> emits top-20 answer-token logprobs; the yes/no log-mass is renormalized to <math id="A1.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the action is blocked iff <math id="A1.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. A block raises a script-level error at the offending line, triggering the fallback hierarchy (agent hand-off, code repair, halt).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verifier and safety guardrails.</span> A safety guardrail confirms that an irreversible action is intended, e.g., a final <span id="A1.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click({concept: "Pay now"})</span>, and is invoked at a small number of known points. The pre-action verifier gates every state-mutating primitive, including reversible ones, against the implicit assumptions under which the line of code was written. A click on an email field is reversible, but if a cookie-consent banner is absorbing pointer events, the click is lost and every later step operates on an unchanged page. We therefore do not skip the check for reversible actions, since a downstream component that could undo a wrong execution may not exist.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verifier and in-code state checks.</span> A code policy may also contain its own state checks, e.g., a <span id="A1.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">stateSatisfies({condition})</span> line inserted where the planner expects a particular state. Three properties separate these from the verifier. First, in-code checks run only where the planner placed them, whereas the verifier runs before every gated primitive. Second, an in-code check carries whatever condition string the planner wrote, which differs across plans and cannot be improved without rewriting the plan, whereas the verifier uses one fixed prompt that we version separately from any code policy. Third, the verifier exposes the threshold <math id="A1.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas an in-code check returns a hard yes or no. We treat in-code checks as a planner affordance for control flow, and they do not replace the verifier.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre-action and post-action checks.</span> Any error that a post-action check on <math id="A1.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> could detect, i.e., a primitive that returned successfully without its intended effect, is also detectable by the pre-action check on <math id="A1.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>, because the precondition of <math id="A1.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> was written against the intended post-state of <math id="A1.SS5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. A pre-action check therefore covers post-action checking up to a lag of one step, uses the same observation as the next action, and leads directly to the fallback, since the response to a failed check is to not execute the next primitive. The final primitive of a plan has no successor to catch its failed effect; the runtime reserves a post-action slot for an outcome check there, and end-of-rollout verification is provided by the task completion judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gated primitives.</span> We gate primitives that write to the state of the computer: pointer and keyboard input, form mutation, navigation, filesystem and clipboard writes, integration writes such as spreadsheet cell updates, and in-page script execution, whether called directly or as a method on an application or page handle. In the ScienceBoard and OSWorld runtime these are <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">double_click</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">type</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">hotkey</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">hold_and_press</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">drag_and_drop</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">set_cell_values</span>, and Python and shell execution. We gate reversible write primitives too, because an undo path may not exist (e.g., a click that triggers an analytics event), and because a skilled human operator would not execute a step against an obviously wrong state regardless of whether the step is reversible. We do not gate read-only primitives (screenshots, accessibility snapshots, reading page content or the clipboard), because they cannot corrupt external state and their outputs are the observations that the verifier consumes. We also do not gate primitives confined to the runtime (variable assignment, control flow, in-memory list operations), whose outcome is determined by the code and cannot disagree with the external world, or window and tab lifecycle operations, which typically run before any observation exists. When membership is ambiguous we gate the primitive, because a spurious check costs one verifier call that usually passes at a low wrong-block operating point. Writes issued through headless APIs, e.g., sending mail through a mail-service API, present no on-screen state to verify against and need a separate safeguard.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inputs.</span> Before executing a gated primitive at step <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the runtime builds the input</p>
<table id="A1.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x_{t}=(g,c_{t},e_{t},o_{t},h_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x_{t}=(g,c_{t},e_{t},o_{t},h_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS5.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the code of the primitive call; <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is a natural-language explanation of the step taken from the in-line comments of the code policy; <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the current observation, as a screenshot, an accessibility tree, or both; and <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> lists the primitives already executed in this run. The verifier <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> maps <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to a decision in <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\text{pass},\text{block}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pass</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>block</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\text{pass},\text{block}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The explanation <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the trailing comment on the statement that contains the call, otherwise the comment block directly above it, otherwise the first line of the enclosing function’s docstring, and otherwise a literal restatement of the call. A verifier note supplies instance-specific knowledge that the verifier cannot infer, e.g., a machine-specific path or the operating system; the note is presented as a fact about the environment and not as approval, so the rubric still applies. The history <math id="A1.SS5.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is a compact list of the steps completed so far in the run, which lets the verifier distinguish a repeated action from its first occurrence without a full transcript.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Log-probability aggregation.</span> We request the 20 most likely next tokens with their log-probabilities at the answer position, skipping any reasoning block that precedes the answer. Let <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}(w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}(w)</annotation></semantics></math> be the log-probability of token <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> at the answer position, restricted to the 20 most likely tokens, and let <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}_{\text{yes}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mtext>yes</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}_{\text{yes}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math> be the surface forms of each answer (e.g., <span id="A1.SS5.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">yes</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Yes</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Y</span>). The probability of blocking is the renormalized mass of the no forms, and the verifier blocks when it reaches a threshold <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> that is set by a calibration set (see Calibration below):</p>
<table id="A1.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle p_{\text{no}}(x_{t})=\frac{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}}\exp\ell_{t}(w)}{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_{\text{yes}}\cup\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}}\exp\ell_{t}(w)},\qquad V_{\theta}(x_{t})=\begin{cases}\text{block}&amp;\text{if }p_{\text{no}}(x_{t})\geq\theta,\\
\text{pass}&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mtext>yes</mtext></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>block</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>pass</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>otherwise</mtext><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle p_{\text{no}}(x_{t})=\frac{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}}\exp\ell_{t}(w)}{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_{\text{yes}}\cup\mathcal{W}_{\text{no}}}\exp\ell_{t}(w)},\qquad V_{\theta}(x_{t})=\begin{cases}\text{block}&amp;\text{if }p_{\text{no}}(x_{t})\geq\theta,\\
\text{pass}&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS5.p6.2" class="ltx_p">The yes forms are <span id="A1.SS5.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">yes</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Yes</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">YES</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">y</span>, <span id="A1.SS5.p6.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Y</span> and their variants with a leading space, and the no forms are defined likewise. We compute the mass of each class with a log-sum-exp over its forms and renormalize over the two classes to obtain <math id="A1.SS5.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#A1.E6" title="In A.5 Pre-action verifier ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). If neither class appears among the 20 tokens, we use the greedy answer, and if the completion contains neither answer, the verifier fails open.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Calibration.</span>

A user who automates a repetitive task expects a working code policy to run without interruption, so a wrong block (stopping a correct primitive) costs more than a wrong pass (running an incorrect primitive), as long as safety guardrails are in place. We therefore set <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> in a calibration phase before any block is enforced. We run the verifier in shadow mode, which computes and logs <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}</annotation></semantics></math> for every gated primitive without enforcing blocks, on a calibration set of rollouts of final policies, and we label each rollout with its task outcome. We treat every primitive of a successful rollout as correct, so any block within a successful rollout is a wrong block. Let <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{WBR}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>WBR</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{WBR}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> be the fraction of successful rollouts in which at least one primitive has <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{DR}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>DR</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{DR}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> the fraction of failed rollouts in which at least one primitive has <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>no</mtext></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{no}}\geq\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. Both rates are non-increasing in <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, so for a wrong-block budget <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> chosen by the deployment, the threshold with the highest detection rate within the budget is the smallest feasible threshold on a grid <math id="A1.SS5.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A1.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\theta^{\ast}=\min\{\theta\in\Theta:\mathrm{WBR}(\theta)\leq\epsilon\}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>WBR</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\theta^{\ast}=\min\{\theta\in\Theta:\mathrm{WBR}(\theta)\leq\epsilon\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Experiment details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Main experiment configuration</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Methods.</span> Both backbones, GPT-5.6 Terra and Claude Opus 5, are called through OpenRouter, and every method on a benchmark uses the same backbone in every LLM role except the judges, the <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">state_satisfies</span> checker, and the continuation summarizer (<a href="#A2.T8" title="In B.1 Main experiment configuration ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). The <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">base agent</em> is Agent-S3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> on OSWorld, with UI-Venus-1.5-30B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2026</a>)</cite> as its grounding model, and ScienceBoard’s own screenshot agent on ScienceBoard. <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">NSPI</em> starts from one base-agent trajectory per task (<a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Initialization ‣ Appendix A Method details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>) and runs policy iteration with <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> iterations of up to <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> rollouts. <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Batch2Code</em> converts three base-agent trajectories per task into a policy with one call of the same converter and no refinement. <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ASI</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> builds its skill library in one online pass over the tasks on top of the same base agent; its later trials replay the agent with the library frozen after that task. Code policies of NSPI and Batch2Code share the grounding model and run under the same step limits.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scoring.</span> Each method gets three fresh trials per task, from which we estimate Pass^k for <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,2,3\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{1,2,3\}</annotation></semantics></math> over the full task set. Cost is the provider-billed model cost plus the grounding model at $3.25 per GPU-hour of call time. One-time construction cost covers conversion and policy iteration (NSPI), conversion (Batch2Code), or the online library-building pass (ASI); per-run cost covers one final trial.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T8" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A2.T8.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
