<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Workflow Variation</h3>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Task variant generation</h4>

<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/task_variant_generation.svg" id="A2.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/168;" width="476" height="168"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>
Given an original target task and environment configuration (initial state and evaluation script), we call an LLM to generate synthetic task variants that differ in the initial state and task parameters
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We generate the variants of each task with one LLM call followed by a deterministic validator (<a href="#A2.F7" title="In B.2.1 Task variant generation ‣ B.2 Workflow Variation ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). The LLM receives the full task specification, i.e., the instruction, the environment setup, and the evaluation script, together with notes that we extract from the evaluation script, e.g., whether it compares the output against a pre-rendered reference file or against inline constants. It first decides for each category whether the task admits variants at all, and then proposes up to three variants per admissible category. An initial-state variant keeps the instruction and adds a setup instruction that a general GUI agent executes before the policy runs, e.g., “Close the spreadsheet window entirely, leaving only the file manager open.” The setup instruction may only change transient application state (open windows, selected tabs, dialogs, etc.) or pre-fill the region that the task writes to, so the files provided by the task setup and the original solution stay unchanged. A parameter variant rewrites the instruction with new argument values and rebinds the constants in the evaluation script to match. The validator rejects a parameter variant if its instruction is unchanged, if the rebound evaluation script uses a different scoring function, or if the script still compares a changed output against the original reference file, because a correct solution could never match that file. It marks variants that pass but carry a warning, e.g., an edited evaluation script on an initial-state variant, for human review. Because the LLM may decline a category, parameter variants are much rarer than initial-state variants: on OSWorld, 332 of 369 tasks pass a pre-filter that removes infeasible tasks, all 332 admit initial-state variants, and only 93 admit parameter variants, mainly because 161 of the other 239 evaluation scripts compare against reference files that we cannot regenerate. We manually review the generated variants and remove infeasible cases. We retain only families whose original task was solved at least once by the Terra or Opus 5 base agent, so failures measure transfer rather than task infeasibility. The resulting benchmark contains 40 parameter families and 35 initial-state families across ten OSWorld domains, generally with three variants per family.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Construction protocol.</span> Both methods use GPT-5.6 Terra for all construction roles and the same grounding model with UI-Venus-1.5-30B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2026)</a></cite>. Variants are processed sequentially while carrying a single policy across the family. Construction starts from each method’s own exploration and never exposes the original task. Only model-judge feedback is available during construction and benchmark evaluators are reserved for final evaluation. NSPI performs up to three refinement iterations with up to three judged rollouts per variant. <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> determines rollout success, while <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{loc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>loc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{loc}}</annotation></semantics></math> provides failure localization for healing. This gated setup was adapted due to the sequential aspect of the experiment meant that lenient judges are more appropriate over strict judges due to the chained dependency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoRPA adaptation.</span> We adapt the AutoRPA reference implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite> to computer-use environments while preserving its exploration, reflection, breakpoint continuation, newest-first verification, and rollback logic. We remove inputs unavailable from a normal user request—the task template, named parameter schema, and benchmark reward. Both methods instead read the current request at execution time, use <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> in place of reward, and share the same visual grounding model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation.</span> After construction on all variants, the policy is frozen and evaluated three times from fresh environments on the original task. If <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> of the three runs succeed, the family contributes <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{c}{k}/\binom{3}{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{c}{k}/\binom{3}{k}</annotation></semantics></math> to Pass^k; results are averaged across families, with construction failures assigned zero.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Judge analysis details</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Annotation.</span> We annotate 19 OSWorld tasks whose initial code policy failed according to <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math>, one rollout per task (<a href="#A2.T9" title="In B.3 Judge analysis details ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). We leave out tasks that fail because a Python library is missing in the guest; these are the most common failures, and the step-level judge cannot see them (see the first limitation). One annotator labels each rollout. The annotator sees the task, the benchmark evaluator, the code policy, one screenshot per step, and the output of every shell command and script. For each rollout, the annotator records five labels: 1) whether the rollout really failed; 2) the divergence step; 3) the first visible divergence, i.e., the first step at which a person who sees only the screenshots can tell that the rollout went wrong, or none if the failure never shows on screen; 4) the type of failure; 5) the cause, in one or two sentences. The annotator then sees the output of the step-level judge and rates it: whether <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> is correct, adjacent (within the same sub-goal), or wrong; whether the narrative names the real cause; whether the suggested focus would steer the healer to the right fix; and whether the observer described the divergence step correctly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ground truth.</span> The annotator judges success against the task instruction and uses the benchmark evaluator as a reference. The two disagree on one rollout, in which the plan wrote network speeds from a command-line tool instead of copying them from the web page that the task names. The evaluator only checks that the file names the three metrics, so it passes the rollout, but the annotator counts it as a failure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task completion judge.</span> <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is correct on 16 of the 19 tasks. The annotator judges the other 3 tasks as successful, so <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> gave false alarms on them. In two of the false alarms, <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> read outdated values from saved files; in the third, it read a default value written by a web tool as a violation of the instruction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step-level judge.</span> We compare <math id="A2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> with the first visible divergence on the 16 confirmed failures. In 6 of them, the failure happens only inside a script and is never visible to the step-level judge; <math id="A2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> is wrong in all 6. In the other 10, the failure becomes visible on screen at some step. Against the first visible divergence, <math id="A2.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> is correct in 7 of these 10, adjacent in 2, and wrong in 1. The narrative names the real cause in 4 of the 10, names it in part in 4, and is wrong in 2. The suggested focus would steer the healer to the right fix in 7 of the 10.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Errors in visible failures.</span> Of the 10 visible failures, <math id="A2.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> misses the first visible divergence in 3. In one, the observer reported no change although a menu failed to open, so <math id="A2.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> points four steps later, where the menu closes. In another, the plan fell one step behind; the judge named the step next to the divergence in its suspect chain but reported a later step as <math id="A2.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the third, the judge matched a condition check to a click in the code, because condition checks write no step-log entry, and placed <math id="A2.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> three steps before the failure shows on screen.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span> We find four limitations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">First, the step-level judge receives no return values from the primitives. It sees the code policy and the screenshots, but not the output of shell commands and scripts or the answers of condition checks, and condition checks appear as screen transitions with no action. This limitation also hides the most common failure, a missing library, because the error appears only in the script output; our sample leaves these failures out, so the counts above are more favorable to the step-level judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Second, when a click misses or registers late, the code policy falls one step behind, and each later action hits the wrong target. The step-level judge then places <math id="A2.SS3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> at the later symptom instead of the step that the healer needs to fix. For instance, a short wait causes the next click to fire before the target has loaded.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Third, neither judge recognizes an infeasible task. Both infeasible tasks in the sample ask for something that does not exist: a “Blue” theme in GIMP and a photo in a folder that has none. Both judges suggest how to complete the task instead of reporting that it is infeasible.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Fourth, <math id="A2.SS3.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{\text{task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>J</mi><mtext>task</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{\text{task}}</annotation></semantics></math> trusts saved files and the output of its own tools more than the running application. Saved files can lag the state of the application, and tool output can contain text that is not in the file.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T9" class="ltx_table">

</span></td></tr>

</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Precondition checks</h3>

<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.36927v1/precondition_wbr.svg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/158;" width="238" height="158"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Pre-action verifier error rates at <math id="A2.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.78</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0.78</annotation></semantics></math>. Rollout-level wrong-block rate on correct policies, by environment, base model used for initial trajectory seed, and verifier model.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The verifier receives a natural-language explanation of each primitive alongside its code. At deployment, the runtime takes this explanation from the comments of the code policy: a trailing comment on the statement that contains the call, otherwise the block of comment lines directly above that statement, otherwise the first line of the docstring of the enclosing function, and otherwise a literal restatement of the call (e.g., “press ctrl+q”, “run a shell command on the VM”). The final code policies produced by policy iteration carry few such comments: on OSWorld with the Terra converter, 99.9% of gated primitives fall back to the literal restatement. A literal restatement gives the verifier no reason for steps that are correct within the plan’s strategy but look destructive in isolation, such as closing an application so that a later step can edit its file on disk. We therefore inject one comment per gated primitive that states the intent of the step within the overall code policy, using the following procedure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Targets.</span> We parse each plan and find every call to a gated primitive (<span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">type</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">hotkey</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">drag_and_drop</span>, <span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">set_cell_values</span>, shell and Python execution, etc.). We group calls by the statement that the runtime uses to look up the explanation, and we leave a statement unchanged if it already has a trailing comment or a comment on the line directly above it, so that existing comments written during refinement are preserved.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intent generation.</span> For each plan we make one call to Gemini 3.8 Flash (low thinking level) with the task instruction, the plan with line numbers, and the target statements, and the model returns one comment per target as JSON. Each comment starts with the action and its target in the words of the code, then explains why the plan takes the step at that point in its strategy. For a step that could look wrong out of context, e.g., closing or killing an application, saving, or running shell code instead of using the GUI, the comment says why the step is needed, and for a close, kill, or save it names the later step that depends on it. A step inside a retry branch is described as retrying an attempt that the preceding check found did not take effect. The comment must not rename or correct the target, claim facts the plan does not establish (e.g., that a file was already saved), or merely restate the call, and it fits on one line of at most 220 characters.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Insertion and verification.</span> The model writes only comments, and a script inserts each one at a fixed position: on the line above the statement for shell and Python execution, whose code argument is usually long or spans several lines, and at the end of the line that ends the call for all other primitives. A call in the condition of an <span id="A2.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">if</span> or <span id="A2.SS4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">while</span> statement gets its comment at the end of the header line, because the runtime’s lookup treats the whole compound statement as the call’s statement and would otherwise find a comment from the body first. We accept the annotated plan only if its abstract syntax tree is unchanged and the runtime’s lookup returns the new comment for every annotated call; otherwise we call the model again, up to four attempts in total, and keep the original plan if none passes. We ran this procedure on the final code policies of OSWorld with the Terra converter (348 plans) and of ScienceBoard with the Opus 5 and Terra converters (159 and 167 plans), and it annotated 673 of the 674 plans with 4,321 comments; the remaining plan does not parse as Python.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verifier inputs.</span> All runs send a fixed note stating that the machine runs Ubuntu with GNOME, where Ctrl- and Alt-based shortcuts are native, because the task instructions given to the verifier do not name the operating system and the rubric blocks shortcuts meant for the wrong operating system. We also evaluate two optional additions to the production rubric. The <em id="A2.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">exemptions</em> address correct plans, whose close, kill, save, and retry steps the production rubric reads as destructive or already done. They state that the following are not by themselves reasons to block: opening or focusing an application, window, or file that is already open; closing or killing an application when the explanation gives a task-related reason, unless the screen shows unsaved work that the step would discard; saving the open document; and repeating a step that the explanation says is a retry, or re-navigating to the page already shown. The <em id="A2.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">blocked targets</em> add two reasons to block that the production rubric missed on perturbed initial states: a shortcut or typed text meant for a specific application while that application is closed, minimized, not in front, or has no document loaded; and any input aimed at a window that a dialog, popup, or menu covers, unless the input is aimed at the dialog itself. With blocked targets, the rubric’s allowance for targets not visible in the screenshot no longer covers these two cases. We report results with and without these additions, since both change the rubric used in production.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>OSWorld-V2 extension</h3>

<div id="A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section records the details of the OSWorld-V2 experiment (<a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Extension to long workflows on OSWorld-V2 ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>) that differ from the OSWorld-Verified and ScienceBoard setup, together with the infrastructure events that affected the runs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmark version and task set.</span> We use the June 2026 release of OSWorld-V2 (<span id="A2.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v2026.06.24</span>), with task definitions, evaluators, and assets unmodified. We report 107 of the 108 tasks. We exclude task 041 because its instruction hard-codes the benchmark authors’ GitLab instance, while setup and grading use the locally deployed one, so no run can be scored as intended. Task 093 is included as a zero for our method, because the converter did not produce a program for it.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Website hosting.</span> 39 of the tasks use web applications that were originally hosted by the benchmark authors. During our experiments, the authors stopped serving the <span id="A2.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v2026.06.24</span> version of these applications and replaced it with a newer version at the same address. The switch happened between 2026-08-25 and 2026-09-10.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base agent.</span> The base agent is a custom harness driving Claude Opus 5 with maximum adaptive thinking and a budget of 500 steps per task, the budget that the benchmark protocol specifies for Claude models. Its seed trajectory for each task comes from run 1.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy construction.</span> The loop follows the refinement algorithm with the settings in <a href="#A2.T10" title="In B.5 OSWorld-V2 extension ‣ Appendix B Experiment details ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. It differs from the OSWorld and ScienceBoard runs in four ways. First, the converter is an agent (Claude Opus 5) that rewrites the seed trajectory into a program, replacing pixel coordinates with element descriptions and deriving task values at run time instead of copying them from the trajectory. Second, the continuation agent is the custom harness running DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with 500 steps and a three-hour wall-clock cap, instead of the base model. Third, the step-level judge receives each rollout as a single transition: the screenshots before and after execution, and the program’s output, capped at its last 50 log entries. It therefore returns a verdict and a failure mode but cannot localize the failure to a step. Fourth, the healer also rewrites the policy after a failure in the last iteration, and the rewritten policy is returned without being judged. As in the other benchmarks, the loop skips the judges and the continuation for rollouts that end in a code execution error.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T10" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>Settings of the OSWorld-V2 construction runs.</figcaption>

<td id="A2.T10.2.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="A2.T10.2.9.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">10 h (exceeding it counts as an infrastructure failure)</span></td></tr>

</table>

<div id="A2.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Infrastructure reruns.</span> We rerun a task only when an infrastructure fault affected its result, never because of a low score, and every completed rerun replaces the original score, including when the score goes down. Task instructions, rubrics, and score weights are unchanged. We ran 13 reruns on tasks with infra failures (004, 005, 010, 018, 021, 024, 025, 058, 061, 073, 089, 092, 100). Of these, four scores went up (004, 025, 092, 100), one went down (061), and eight were unchanged. Tasks whose reruns are still running keep their original scores.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cost.</span> Construction cost $8.2 per task on average in LLM calls (Opus 5 58%, Sonnet 4.6 30%, DeepSeek 9%, Gemini 3%) and a median of 2.9 VM-hours per task. Counting infrastructure reruns, total LLM spend was <math id="A2.SS5.p7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.8\times</annotation></semantics></math> that amount. Grounding calls and LLM calls inside official evaluators are not metered. We estimate script costs during execution due to LLM calls to be $0.03–$0.08 on average.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Constructing Policies from Unsuccessful Trajectories</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine whether NSPI can build a working policy from an unsuccessful trajectory. We split the runs by whether the selected seed trajectory <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> succeeds under the benchmark evaluation script. A failed seed is from tasks on which the base agent fails all three attempts. The resulting split represents how NSPI behaves when it starts from a successful versus an unsuccessful demonstration of the task.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We find that NSPI can construct reliable policies from unsuccessful trajectories to a substantial degree as shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Reliability across repeated executions ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Neuro-Symbolic Computer Use: Learning Reusable Policies for Reliable and Efficient Execution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Across the 356 policies built from a failed seed, 62 succeed in all three final runs under the benchmark evaluator, reflecting policies that are consistently correct rather than occasionally lucky. On tasks with a successful seed, the final plan also improves over the base agent in three of the four settings, indicating that NSPI generally adds reliability even when a correct demonstration is already available.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recovering from a failed seed is more costly than refining a successful one. Failed seeds cost 18–31% more and take 17–38% longer to reach a policy than successful seeds, and in three of four settings they receive a larger share of judge rejections during policy iteration . This is consistent with the intuition that a failed trajectory contains more incorrect or missing steps that must be diagnosed and repaired before the resulting policy passes the judges.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>
